text:
Chapter five. The stress test.

Now the real experiment. What would a crash do to the portfolios people actually hold today?

I split the world index into four buckets.

The AI giants, about twenty-five percent. The rest of the US, about forty-six. Other developed markets, about twenty-nine. And for global funds, emerging markets.

Why a separate bucket for the AI giants? Because if this is a bubble, that's where it is. The chips, the cloud, the data centres. That's the money betting on AI.

Then I ran two scenarios, based on what really happened in past crashes. These are scenarios, not forecasts.

Scenario A: an AI-only correction. The AI giants fall fifty percent. The rest of the US falls ten. Other markets dip a little.

Scenario B: a full dot-com replay. The AI giants lose seventy percent, and like in 2000, everything else falls hard too.

The maths is deliberately simple. For each portfolio, I multiplied its weight in each bucket by that bucket's loss, and added it all up. You could redo it on a napkin.

Scenario B isn't made up. From 2000 to 2002, the big tech names of that era lost seventy to ninety percent. The S and P five hundred lost about half. And as we saw, Europe lost about two thirds.

Let's start with scenario A. A plain M S C I World ETF loses about eighteen and a half percent.

Now, many people think: I'll switch to an All-World fund, with emerging markets. That gets you to minus eighteen point two. Almost no difference.

Why? Because emerging markets are full of AI too. Taiwan and Korea are home to some of the biggest chipmakers on the planet.

An equal weight world fund, where every company gets the same slice, loses only seven percent.

Europe only: minus five. And a sixty forty portfolio, sixty percent world stocks and forty percent euro government bonds: minus nine.

Equal weight does well here for an obvious reason: the AI giants are just a handful of names out of more than thirteen hundred. In an equal weight fund, they're less than one percent of your money.

But remember, Europe has its own giants too. A few companies like A S M L, S A P and Novo Nordisk drive a big part of European returns. Concentration isn't only an American thing.

In an AI-only correction, the alternatives really work. But now, scenario B.

M S C I World: minus forty-five percent. All-World: also minus forty-five.

Equal weight: minus thirty-eight. Europe only: minus forty.

And the sixty forty: minus twenty-four.

This is the uncomfortable result. In a real crash, switching from one stock index to another barely matters. The only thing that really changed the outcome was owning something that isn't stocks.

That doesn't make equal weight or All-World bad ideas. They spread your bets more evenly. Since 2000, equal weight even edged out the standard world index, about seven point eight percent a year versus seven point five, in dollars. They're just not crash protection.

And we don't have to guess. Here's the real sixty forty, replayed from the end of 1999, with yearly rebalancing.

At the end of 2002, it was down twenty-one percent instead of forty-five.

It was back above ten thousand euros in 2005. Eight years earlier than the all-stock portfolio.

The price? Today it's worth about thirty-eight thousand six hundred, instead of forty-six thousand. Less growth, in exchange for much smaller holes.

There's a hidden engine in that sixty forty: rebalancing. Every year it goes back to sixty percent stocks. So at the end of 2002 and 2008, it was forced to sell bonds and buy cheap stocks. Exactly when nobody wanted to.

But there's a warning label. In 2022, euro government bonds lost about eighteen percent, in the same year stocks fell.

Bonds protected you in 2000 and 2008, when interest rates fell. They don't protect you when inflation and rates are rising. And inflation in the euro area is back above three percent.

And one more honest point. Over the last decade, almost every one of these safer alternatives trailed the plain world index. Protection always has a price.
